“April 7. I rose early and, to my immense delight, finally saw what could only be the North Pole itself. It lay unmistakably right beneath my feet. Unfortunately, I had now climbed so far that I could make out no precise details. Indeed, judging from the progression of my recorded altitudes between six in the morning of April 2 and twenty minutes to nine that same morning, when the barometer ran down, a reasonable calculation placed the balloon at least 7,254 miles above sea level by four this morning, April 7. That height may seem enormous, but the estimate behind it probably produced a figure well below the truth. In any case, I could unquestionably see the earth’s full major diameter. The whole northern hemisphere spread beneath me like a map projected from directly above, while the great circle of the equator marked the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies can easily imagine, however, that the limited unexplored areas within the Arctic Circle remained comparatively tiny and too distant for close examination. This was true even though they lay directly below me and therefore appeared without foreshortening. Nevertheless, what I could see was strange and exciting. North of the enormous rim already described, which could with minor qualifications be called the boundary of human discovery in these regions, stretched a continuous or nearly continuous ice sheet. Across its first few degrees, the surface became noticeably flatter; farther on, it sank into a plane. Finally, curving inward quite distinctly, it ended at the Pole in a sharply outlined circular center. Seen from the balloon, this center’s diameter covered an angle of about sixty-five seconds of arc. Its dark color varied in intensity but was always darker than any other part of the visible hemisphere, sometimes deepening into complete, impenetrable blackness. Little more could be established. By noon the circular center had shrunk considerably, and by seven that evening it had vanished from sight. The balloon had crossed the western edge of the ice and was drifting rapidly toward the equator.

“April 8. I noticed a clear decrease in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a considerable change in its overall color and appearance.

I got up early and once again managed to slip past the people to whom I owed money. Eagerly, I went to the bookseller’s stall and spent my little remaining cash on books about mechanics and practical astronomy. After bringing them safely home, I used every spare moment to study them. Before long, I believed I had learned enough to carry out my plan. During this time, I also made every effort to win over the three creditors who had troubled me so much. Eventually I succeeded, partly by selling enough furniture to pay half their claims, and partly by promising the rest when I completed a small project I said I was planning. I asked them to help with it. They were uneducated men, and these methods made it fairly easy to gain their support.

“With that settled, my wife helped me secretly and cautiously sell my remaining property. I also borrowed a considerable amount of cash in small sums, giving various reasons and paying no attention to how I might repay it. With this money I gradually bought pieces of very fine cambric muslin, twelve yards long; string; a supply of rubber varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and other items needed to build and equip an unusually large balloon. I told my wife to make it as quickly as possible and gave her all the instructions she needed. Meanwhile, I worked the string into a net of the proper size and fitted it with a hoop and the necessary cords. I bought a quadrant, a compass, a telescope, an ordinary barometer with some important changes, and two less familiar astronomical instruments. Then, whenever I could do so at night, I transported materials to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam. These included five iron-bound barrels holding about fifty gallons each and one larger barrel; six suitably shaped tubes of tin-coated metal, each three inches wide and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metal or semi-metal that I will not name; and twelve large glass containers of a very common acid. The gas produced from the last two materials has never been made by anyone but me—or at least never used for a purpose like this. I would readily reveal the secret, except that it rightfully belongs to a man from Nantz in France, who shared it with me under certain conditions.

Raymond paced angrily across the room. I stood ready to hear his accusations and answer them. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is utterly ridiculous,” he exclaimed. “Even schoolboys could not behave more irrationally.”

“You don’t understand,” Raymond said. “This is part of a whole system, a plan of tyranny I will never accept. Must being Protector of England make me the empire’s only slave? My privacy invaded, my conduct criticized, my friends insulted? I will rid myself of all of it. Witness this.” He pulled the star, the symbol of his office, from his chest and threw it onto the table. “I resign my office. I surrender my power. Whoever wants it can take it!”

“Let it go,” Adrian cried, “to anyone who calls himself, or whom the world calls, a better man than you. Nobody in England has the arrogance to make that claim. Understand yourself, Raymond, and your anger will pass; your confidence will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for our country’s prosperity or our own, we prayed too for the Protector’s life and happiness, knowing them to be inseparable. You spent your days working for our benefit; your ambition was to earn our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, established useful institutions, and made our land abundantly fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your judgment, while the poor and oppressed rose like flowers waking in the morning sunlight of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we are shocked and saddened when all this seems to have changed? But come, this burst of anger has already passed. Return to your duties. Your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will fall silent, and we will again show you our love, respect, and loyalty. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world will answer to you.”

“That would be excellent advice for someone else,” Raymond answered gloomily. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the country’s foremost nobleman, may become its ruler. Good, wise, and just as you are, you could command every heart. But I realize, too soon for my own happiness and too late for England’s benefit, that I accepted a task beyond my strength. I cannot govern myself. My passions command me; my slightest impulse is a tyrant. Do you think I abandoned the Protectorate—and I have abandoned it—in a passing fit of anger? By the living God, I swear never to pick up that trinket again, never again to carry the burden of anxiety and misery that it represents.
